en: Preface to the Daily Use of a Śramaṇa One who awakens the mind and penetrates the fundamental source is called a śramaṇa. Such a person fulfills the three thousand majestic deportments and upholds the eighty thousand subtle practices.

This present work, *Daily Use*, is the pivotal essence of those three thousand deportments and the wondrous application of those eighty thousand practices. For those who have left the household life and seek advancement...

It is the ladder for cultivation and the compassionate vessel by which Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings. If the ladder is lost and the compassionate vessel is lacking, how can there be self-benefit or the benefit of others?
The title "Daily Use of the Vinaya" (Bini Riyong) is an error; *Vinaya* is the same as *Lü* (the Vinaya).
It is the Vinaya-piṭaka among the Five Piṭakas, clarifying solely the two hundred and fifty precepts for Bhikṣus, and does not speak of the various [esoteric] truths.

Regarding the incantations (*dhāraṇī*) and the verses interspersed therein, many are drawn from the *Avataṃsaka* and various other sūtras; as for the incantations themselves, they are recorded in the Esoteric Section (*Guhyamantra-vinaya*).

Nevertheless, the sūtras, the vinaya, and the mantras each have their own distinct purposes; how could they be allowed to be confused or intermingled? How could one then designate the vinaya as the primary authority for them?

Now, our Master, residing as an upādhyāya, is truly a pillar of support in the Dharma-ending age and a skilled physician for saving the world; he has provided commentaries on both the sūtras and the vinaya.

It comprises more than one hundred fascicles and includes various incantations. Regarding both Chinese and Sanskrit terms, as well as foreign languages, there is nothing he has not thoroughly mastered.
Lamenting the declining customs of the Dharma-ending age and pitying the ignorance of future generations, he proceeded to revise and edit [the texts], titling the work *The Daily Use of a Śramaṇa*.

The names and realities correspond perfectly; the matters are concise while the principles are detailed. Although this is addressed to śramaṇas, all lay male and female faithful who have received the refuges and precepts and embrace the bodhisattva dharma must practice it.

It is intended that the seven assemblies, throughout the two periods of six times [day and night], whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, shall dedicate even a single hair’s breadth of merit toward all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, so that they may together transcend [suffering].
This is the "Essence of Suffering" (Kujin), which completes the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Six Perfections and the myriad deeds.

Now, at the end of the section on daily observances (*vinaya*) in various regions, there are further added the words of admonition by ancient masters. While it may be said that this constitutes some small measure of merit, these words of the ancient masters—

These are recorded in their respective biographies; how could they be indiscriminately merged? To do so would lose the meaning of the *vinaya* and greatly violate the intent of the sūtras and vinayas.
Let those with discernment distinguish them.
Written by the disciple Kaiding on the day of the *pravāraṇa* ceremony in the Xinhai year of the Kangxi era, at Zhuyue Lou in Dinghu.
*The Daily Activities of a Śramaṇa*, Volume One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baixianglin Monastery in Nanhai, Guangzhou. Now, as for those who are śramaṇas:
they diligently practice all manner of goodness and bring to rest all deluded thoughts. Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, their bodies...

Clad in the four modes of deportment, holding both Exoteric and Esoteric teachings in one’s mouth, and dwelling with concentration and wisdom in the mind, the three mysteries thus become harmonized and the myriad practices gradually perfected.

Therefore, the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* instructs all Bodhisattvas that whatever they do, they should always generate vows and dedicate the merit so that all sentient beings may together attain perfect enlightenment; this is the means of benefiting both oneself and others.
This is the fundamental vow of the Great Being (Mahāsattva). Although it is said that he currently dwells in the realm of ordinary beings, he has already perfected the practices of a sage.
Examining these daily applications, their origins are not uniform; they are all compilations from this region, and thus the names and titles differ in many ways.

The various sections contain some discrepancies; among them, many of the verses are taken from the *Śīla-varga* (Chapter on Pure Conduct), while the mantras and incantations are all recorded from the various scriptures of the Secret Section (*Guhyatantra*).
However, as for this compilation, its breadth and brevity lack propriety; I have now adjusted it to find a middle ground.

I have edited and supplemented this into a complete volume for students to uphold and recite. As for the light and heavy precept categories of the Bodhisattva, they are fully detailed in the sutras and śāstras;

as for the five sections and seven groups of the Bhikṣu, they are exhaustively contained within the Vinaya Piṭaka. One should naturally investigate these thoroughly to understand what is to be ceased and what is to be practiced, as well as what constitutes upholding and what constitutes transgression.
One must not consider the task finished merely by relying on this [text]. Recently, I have observed that certain masters of our time...

They do not consult the Vinaya scriptures nor rely upon them to perform repentance for their transgressions; they merely require that one recite a certain number of mantras. This completely contradicts the teachings on confession and disclosure.

How can they know that the Exoteric and Esoteric traditions differ, and that each form of repentance has its own specific purpose? If one does not repent according to the Vinaya, their offenses cannot be escaped.

To err oneself and cause others to err is a fault no small matter; let the wise be cautious in this regard. (Although these are said to be the daily practices of śramaṇas, they are likewise observed by lay bodhisattvas.)
Upper Section: The Gate of Recitation ○ Upon Waking from Sleep (When the practitioner awakens from sleep,
they should immediately sit upright with the body straightened and silently recite the following verse and mantra:)
Upon first awakening from sleep, one should wish that all sentient beings awaken to all-encompassing wisdom and survey the ten directions.
Oṃ dhṛti dhīri svāhā (seven times).
[Hearing the bell]
(When the practitioner hears the sound of the bell, they should recite this verse and mantra:
Hearing the sound of the bell, Afflictions grow light, Wisdom increases, And Bodhi arises.
Leaving the hells behind, Escaping the fiery pit, May I attain Buddhahood To deliver all sentient beings.

Oṃ. Karateye svāhā. (Recite seven times. Whenever one hears the sound of a bell, one should immediately rise from one's seat. If one gives way to indolence, one invites fault upon oneself. The *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* states: "If one hears the bell and remains lying down without rising, the protective deity of the bed will become resentful;
in this life there will be no merit or wisdom, and after death one will fall into the body of a snake. However, if one is severely ill, there is no fault in not rising. )
Striking the bell, one makes this vow: May the sound of this bell transcend the Dharma-realm, so that it may be heard throughout the dark recesses of the Iron Ring Mountains;
may the auditory faculty be purified through this hearing, realizing perfect penetration, and may one attain true enlightenment in a single thought of pure mind. (Recite the mantra as before.)
Upon waking and rising (rising from the bed and standing upright, recite):
When placing my feet upon the ground, may all sentient beings attain liberation of mind and abide in immovability.
(Next, recite: From the morning dawn until evening, may all sentient beings protect themselves;
if any should lose their lives beneath my feet, I pray that you be reborn immediately in the Pure Land.
Oṃ, Eḍidulani svāhā. (Recite seven times.)
○ Putting on Clothes (When putting on clothes after descending from the bed, one should recite):
If putting on the upper garment, I vow that all sentient beings May obtain supreme roots of goodness And reach the further shore of the Dharma.
When putting on the lower garment, one should wish that all beings clothe themselves in all roots of goodness and be fully endowed with a sense of shame and remorse.
When adjusting the robes and fastening the belt, one should wish that all beings restrain their roots of goodness so as not to let them be lost or scattered.
When walking, one should wish...
(When lifting the foot to walk, recite:
When lifting the foot, may all sentient beings be born beyond the sea of birth and death and be endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
(Then recite the mantra for walking without harming insects and ants:)
Oṃ dhiri dhiri svāhā (seven times).
○ Rinsing the mouth (when washing the face upon rising in the morning, one should recite as follows):
Washing the face with water, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the gate of pure Dharma and be forever free from defilement.
Oṃ raṃ (twenty-one times) svāhā. (When washing the face upon rising, one must chew a *dantakāṣṭha* [tooth-stick]. The verse and mantra are as follows.
○ Drinking Water.
(The Buddha observed the water in a single bowl and saw eighty-four thousand insects. He said, "If one does not recite this mantra, it is as if one were eating the flesh of sentient beings.
The mantra is: Oṃ vaśīvara maṇi svāhā. (Recite seven times.
○ Don the five robes.
(One should recite the verse and mantra as follows:
Excellent is this robe of liberation, The supreme field of merit garment. I now receive it upon my head;
May I never be parted from it in life after life.
Oṃ siddhya svāhā (seven times).
○ Donning the seven robes (one should recite the verse and mantra as follows):
Excellent is the garment of liberation, the supreme field of merit robe. I now receive it upon my head;
may I always wear it in every life. Oṃ. Tāra tāra. Svāhā. (Recite seven times.)
○ When donning the great robe (one should recite the verse and dhāraṇī as follows):
Excellent is this garment of liberation, The supreme field of merit; I now receive it upon my head.
To extensively deliver all deluded beings:
Oṃ mahākā papoṭa siddhe svāhā. (Recite seven times; alternatively, one may use the following verse for the three robes.
When donning the kāṣāya robe, I vow that all sentient beings: May their minds be unstained by defilement, And fully realize the Way of the Great Sage.
When a śrāmaṇera puts on the *māṇavaka* robe (he should recite this verse):
How great is the garment of liberation! The signless field of merit robe; I don it and honor it as my practice of the precepts.
To widely deliver all those who are deluded:

Regarding the *maṇḍa* robe (*maṇḍa-cīvara*), "maṇḍa" refers to a single piece of cloth, lacking the characteristics of being cut into strips or partitioned by seams. All who receive the ten precepts wear this garment. However, because of the corruption of the Dharma at the end of the age, people have failed to understand the robes that a śramaṇa ought to wear.

This error has been transmitted for so long that they have followed one another in practice until śrāmaṇeras are now wearing the five- or seven-strip robes of a bhikṣu. Therefore, the *Mūla-karman* states: "The attire of those seeking tranquility (śrāmaṇeras) is the *maṇḍa*-strip robe; yet some arbitrarily wear the five-strip robe."

This is a profound perversion and abuse. In the land of China, this custom has long been propagated; it constitutes an unrighteous practice and must not be worn. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-karmavācanā* was personally translated in this region by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing, who traveled to the Western Regions.

Since he stated that "corrupt customs have long been propagated" and that "this decay has not been a matter of a single day," and yet we remain unawakened to this day—who will set us right? We rely specifically on great Bodhisattvas who propagate the Dharma to dispel the confusion of a thousand ages, open the eyes of wisdom for those to come, ensure that the True Dharma endures for a long time, and allow the pearl of the precepts to be eternally polished.
○ Paying Homage to the Buddha (When intending to go to pay homage to the Buddha, one should recite this verse and mantra):
If I am fortunate enough to behold the Buddha, I vow that all sentient beings May attain the unobstructed eye And see all Buddhas.
Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ (seven times; the syllable *pha* is half a mora).
○ Entering the Buddha Hall (If entering a hall or a ritual site, one should recite this verse and mantra):
If entering a hall or chamber, one should wish that all sentient beings ascend the unsurpassed hall and dwell therein immovably.
Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ. (Recite seven times; the syllable *pha* has half a mora.
◎ Contemplating the Buddha.
(If one sees a Buddha image, one should contemplate it with a sincere and attentive mind. One should recite this verse:
When contemplating the Buddha, may all sentient beings become like Samantabhadra—exquisite, upright, and majestic.
I pay homage to the Triple Gem.

(Whenever performing prostrations, one must first praise their virtues. As for these words of praise, they must be taken from the verses found within the sūtras and śāstras. Having finished praising, call upon the name [of the Buddha]. Then, cast the five limbs to the ground and let both hands reach toward the air, demonstrating the gesture of receiving the feet.
This constitutes the visualization of Mañjuśrī Prostrating to the Buddha; therein, one should cultivate the following mental imagery).
The nature of the worshiper and the object of worship is empty and quiescent; the mutual resonance of their paths is inconceivable.
My place of practice is like a jewel of Indra, within which the reflections of all Buddhas of the ten directions appear.
My own reflection appears before all those Buddhas; with my head meeting their feet, I take refuge and pay homage.

(If paying homage to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas individually, simply change the two characters "zhū fó" [all Buddhas]. If paying homage to the Sangha, one should say: "Within the manifestation of the worthy and holy ones of the ten directions. If paying homage to the Dharma, one should say:).
The dharma-nature of true emptiness is like space; The eternally abiding jewel of Dharma is inconceivable.
My own shadow-form appears before the jewel of Dharma; With single-minded devotion, I take refuge and pay homage according to the Dharma.
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, one should next pay homage to the Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, and Maitreya...
Having prostrated one by one before Buddha Rocana, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and all the great Bodhisattvas,
as well as the Venerable Kāśyapa, Upāli, and Ānanda, you should with a sincere mind perform repentance, entreaty, and sympathetic joy.
The texts for dedication and making vows are fully detailed in various sūtras as well as in the "Chapter on Vows and Conduct" (Pranidhāna-paṭala); they are not recorded here at length.
(The verses of praise and the ritual procedures for prostrating to the Buddha are briefly provided.)

○ Paying Homage to the Stūpa (The term "stūpa" is rendered in full as *stūpa* in Sanskrit; it is also called *sūtra-pa*, *pīṭhaka*, or *caitya*. This is translated as "accumulation of marks," meaning that the manifold virtues of the Tathāgata are all gathered therein. Sometimes it contains relics.)

Alternatively, there may be no relics. Where there are no relics, one should install a verse of the Dharmakāya or an image of the Tathāgata. By paying homage to it, one extinguishes immeasurable sins and generates immeasurable merit. When seeing a stūpa, one should say:
When seeing a Buddha stūpa, one should wish that all sentient beings be honored like a stūpa and receive offerings from devas and humans.
(When performing prostrations, one should recite this verse:)
I prostrate before the stūpa; may all sentient beings—every human and every deva—be such that none can see their crown.

(Having prostrated, one should circumambulate three times, or seven times, ten times, a hundred times, or a thousand times. One must keep track of the number of circumambulations, as each has its specific significance: for instance, three circumambulations symbolize the extinguishing of the three poisons and the perfecting of the three virtues; seven circumambulations purify the seven branches of ethical discipline.)

One attains the seven factors of enlightenment, severs the ten latent tendencies (anuśaya) with ten circumambulations, and realizes the ten powers (bala). The rest should be understood by analogy. When circumambulating a stūpa, one should recite as follows:
Circumambulating the stūpa to the right, one should wish that all sentient beings act without opposition and attain all-encompassing wisdom.
(When circumambulating three times, one should say:)
Circumambulating the stupa three times, one should wish that all sentient beings diligently seek the Buddha-way with minds free from weariness.
(Next, recite the Dharani for Circumambulating the Stupa to Extinguish Sins:)
Namo buddhāya | Namo dharmāya | Namo saṃghāya | Namo āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā...
*Tatha*, *khara-vadhi*, *sukha-vadhi*, *gava-dhi*. (Recite these seven times, then circumambulate to the right.

If one can, with a sincere mind and single-pointed focus, circumambulate the stupa and practice walking meditation for seven days, reciting [the mantra] twelve thousand times, one will behold the majestic power of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva face-to-face, extinguish all karmic obstacles, and attain all one’s aspirations.

According to the Vinaya regulations, one must not cover the head, but should wear the robe over both shoulders and, if wearing a meditation robe, leather sandals, and so forth, when prostrating to the Buddha or circumambulating the stupa.)
Chanting the Sūtras (When chanting the sūtras, one should first recite this verse):
While reciting the sūtras, may all sentient beings follow what the Buddha has taught, maintaining total retention without forgetfulness.
Holding the Khakkhara (When holding the khakkhara, one should first recite this verse and mantra):
Holding the khakkhara staff, I vow that all sentient beings May establish great assemblies of giving And reveal the path of reality as it is.
Oṃ. Naḷica naḷica naḷitapate naḷitānaya bhaṇi hūṃ phaṭ (seven times; the syllable *pha* has half a mora).
○ Begging for alms.
(When about to enter a village for alms, one must first recite this verse:
Setting out upon the path, I vow that all sentient beings May follow the conduct of the Buddhas And enter the state of non-reliance.
(While walking on the road, one should say:)
If one is on the road, one should wish that all sentient beings may be able to practice the Buddha-way and turn toward the Dharma of no-remainder (when entering a village, one should say this).
Entering a village to beg for alms, one should wish that all sentient beings enter the profound Dharma-realm with minds free from obstruction.
(The old practice used the Cundī Dhāraṇī, but as it has no canonical source, it is not recorded here. When arriving at the door, one should say:)
Upon entering a person’s door, one should wish that all beings enter the gateway of all Buddha-dharmas.
(Once having entered their home, one should say:)
Having entered their home, one should wish that all beings may enter the Buddha-vehicle and attain equality throughout the three periods of time.
(If they do not abandon [their ways], one should not give rise to a mind of anger or vexation; rather, one should say:)
Upon seeing one who does not abandon others, one should wish that all beings never forsake the dharmas of supreme merit (and,
upon seeing one who practices giving, should not become greedily attached).
Upon seeing one who is capable of renunciation, one should wish that all sentient beings may forever attain liberation from the sufferings of the three evil realms.
Upon seeing an empty bowl (if,
when about to eat, one sees an empty bowl, one should recite this verse):
If one sees an empty bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings have pure minds, empty and free from afflictions.
When unfolding the bowl at mealtime (before receiving food, first unfold the bowl to make it clean; at that time, one should recite this verse):
The Tathāgata is the vessel of measure; now I have obtained the opportunity to spread forth [offerings]. May I provide for all beings, together realizing the emptiness of the three spheres.
(Seeing the bowl filled.)
(If one sees a bowl filled with food, one should recite this verse:
If one sees a full bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings May fully accomplish and perfect All wholesome dharmas.
(The three verses above were forcibly inserted into this text from other sources by the old edition; as they have no canonical provenance, they are not recorded here.)
○ Upon obtaining fine food (if one obtains fine food and drink, one should recite this verse): If one obtains fine food,
One should wish that all sentient beings May have their aspirations fulfilled And that their minds be free from covetous desire.
○ When obtaining unwholesome food (if one obtains unwholesome food or drink, one should recite this verse):
Obtaining unwholesome food, I vow that all sentient beings May never fail to obtain The flavor of all samādhis.
○ Holding the Alms Bowl (When holding the bowl, one should recite the verse and mantra):
Holding the vessel of the worthy recipient, I vow that all sentient beings shall perfect the vessel of the Dharma and receive offerings from devas and humans.
Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ (seven times; the *pha* sound is half a mora).

According to the Vinaya regulations, when eating in a large assembly, one should set aside a single dish at the end of the line to provide for the Mother of the Ghost Children (*Hārītī*) and her retinue. One should call out their names so that they may all be fully satisfied; it is also excellent to invoke them with the aforementioned verse. However, current practices are merely local corruptions and have no basis in the Buddha’s regulations. To place a small amount of food in an impure location and call upon the names of great ghosts and spirits not only provides no benefit, but is feared to invite misfortune. Furthermore, the Vinaya prescribes that when the meal invited by a donor is finished, one should briefly purify the hands and mouth with water. Section on Requisites, Part Two—
The Names and Characteristics of the Three Robes.
First is the *antarvāsa* (Sanskrit). This is translated here as the "lower garment," also called the "overnight garment," the "inner garment," or the "undergarment.
It refers to that which is worn close to the body; it is the garment for walking within the monastery grounds and for miscellaneous tasks.
Second is the *uttarāsaṅga*. This is called the "upper garment," meaning it is the highest among those garments normally worn.
It is also called the "garment for entering the assembly," meaning it is worn on such occasions as paying respects, reciting scriptures, eating, and listening to lectures.
The *tricīvara* (three-fold robe). This is translated as "layered" (*chóng*) or "joined" (*hé*), meaning it is made by cutting [a large cloth] and joining the pieces together to form layers.

It is also called the "variegated fragmentary robe" (*zásuì yī*), because it consists of many strips. It is also called the "repeated-layered robe" (*chóngfù yī*). When entering a royal palace, [one should wear this].
When entering a village, begging for food, eating, warding off the cold, preaching the Dharma, or paying homage to a stūpa, one should wear these robes.
These three robes are collectively called *cīvara* in India; if designated by their color, they are all termed *kāṣāya*.
The Buddha said: "The disciples of the Buddhas of the past and future shall all wear these robes, just as I do today. [They are cut] with a blade.
[The robes] are cut into garments so as not to be plundered by enemies or thieves. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (*Sapoduo lun*) states:

"The reason for establishing these distinctions in the names of the three robes is the desire to manifest an unprecedented teaching (*anupūrva-dharma*). Among all ninety-six [non-Buddhist] schools, the names of these three robes do not exist;
thus, these distinctions are made because they differ from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The *Gongde lun* states: "To create the three..."
Regarding "robes": it is because of the turning of the Wheel of Dharma in three revolutions; again, it is said, for the sake of the three periods of time;
and again, it is said, for the sake of the three seasons. In winter one wears heavy ones; in summer one wears light ones; and in spring one wears medium ones.
During times of great cold, one may wear the three robes layered heavily to provide protection. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the Buddha said: "The three robes are the [attire] of a śramaṇa."
These are the insignia of the noble ones. Therefore, my disciples, with these three robes, are fully able to ward off great cold and great heat, as well as flies and gadflies;

they provide a covering for shame and modesty, and do not destroy the lineage of the sages. For those whose nature cannot endure the cold, I permit them to take old, worn-out garments and have them quilted as they wish;
this is precisely what is meant by having few desires and few concerns. The *Jie tan jing* (Sutra on the Precept Platform) says: "The five-strip lower robe..."
The seven-strip inner robe (*antarvāsaka*) severs greed of the body; the twenty-five-strip outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) severs anger of the mouth; and [the nine-strip robe] severs delusion of the mind.
Regarding the method of cutting and construction, as stated in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*: "The three robes collectively comprise three grades."
Regarding the *saṃghāṭī*, the superior grade is measured by one's own cubits: three spans in height and five spans in width. The inferior grade reduces each dimension by half a cubit;
those between these two are called the intermediate grade. The *uttarāsaṅga* and the *antarvāsaka* also have three grades, and their measurements are identical to this.

Regarding those whose bodies are tall but whose elbows are short, the measurement is based on the body and not on the elbow. Conversely, for those who are the opposite, it is likewise based on the body.
As for the number of strips and the method of partitioning the tiers: the *antarvāsa* (inner robe) has five strips, with one long and one short;
the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) has seven strips, with two long and one short; and as for the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe), there are nine varieties of strip counts.
They differ as follows: namely, nine strips, eleven strips, thirteen strips, fifteen strips, seventeen strips, nineteen strips, twenty-one strips, twenty-three strips, and twenty-five strips.
Regarding the altar partitions (*maṇḍala-vedikā*): for the first three [sections], two are long and one is short;
for the next three, three are long and one is short; for the final four, four are long and one is short. Beyond this, they increase accordingly.
It thus becomes a patched robe (*pāṃsukūla*). Because it cannot be worn as is, its method of sewing and patching follows the pattern of rice-field ridges;
the strips (*khaṇḍa*) are cut so that they face both sides and do not lean in a single direction. There are three distinctions among these strips: superior, middling, and inferior.

The superior are four finger-widths wide, narrowing to two finger-widths at the edges; those between these two measurements are called middling. Generally, when making a small altar, one should follow the proportions of a large altar.
Half [of the leaf]. However, when cutting the small altar cloth relative to the large altar cloth, one must further increase it by half a leaf.

Only after completing the first seam will the light and dark [patterns] be clearly manifested and properly correspond. Anything other than this is incorrect. The *Neifa zhuan* (Biographies of the Inner Dharma) states:
"The dharma robes of the five regions of India may be either embroidered or sewn; the inner leaf and outer border are each one inch wide, and the outer border has embroidery."
Regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*), the inner flaps are all sewn together. Furthermore, in the Western Regions, the three robes are all embroidered with flaps to be joined;
it is only in the Land of the East (China) that they are left open and not sewn. Upon a detailed examination of the Vinaya texts, there is truly no method for leaving them open.

I personally inquired among the various countries of the north where the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is practiced; in all cases, the flaps are embroidered together, and none leave them open. If it were so in the West...
Having obtained the Dharma robes of the Divine Land (China), one sews them together before donning them. All the Vinaya texts of the various schools state that they should be "stitched together.
Master Daoxuan asked a celestial being: "Recently, I have seen many Western Region monks arriving who wear their robe-pieces merely sewn together; why is this? The being replied:
Two hundred years after this Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, a monk from North India lived together with non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas).
The outsiders became jealous of him and secretly placed a sharp knife inside the folds of his inner robe. They went together to the king's presence, where the outsiders informed the king:

"This Śramaṇa son of the Śākya family has concealed a sharp knife within himself, intending to harm Your Majesty. Consequently, he was arrested and investigated; because of this, he was executed along with many others.

Regarding the monks of a certain country: at that time, there was the Arhat Yaśas, who instructed the monks to temporarily sew [the robes closed) as a provisional measure against the danger of losing their lives.
This was a temporary regulation established by him due to specific circumstances in that region; it was not something authorized by the Buddha. (According to these two accounts...)

As for sewing, this conforms to the Vinaya texts of the various schools; as for not sewing, this is based on what was spoken by devas and humans. One may adopt either method, as there is no contradiction with reason. Furthermore, regarding the construction of waterways nowadays, there is no textual authority in the various Vinayas;

it was originally not ordained by the Buddha, but is a local invention of this region. Or perhaps it is a clever fabrication based on a mistaken interpretation of the teachings of Nanshan (Daoxuan), such as the practice of attaching patches to robes and arbitrarily claiming they represent Mount Sumeru, the sun and moon, or the Heavenly Kings.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "For new robes, one layer is permitted for the *antaravāsaka* and the *uttarāsaṅga*; two layers are permitted."
Regarding the *saṃghāṭī*: if it is a garment made from old cloth, it is permitted to make it double-layered for the five- or seven-strip robe, and four-layered for the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*).
If it is a *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe), the number of layers may be as many or few as desired. The *Nèfǎ chuán* (Inner Dharma Tradition) states:

regarding the method for wearing the robes and fastening the ties and loops, one may take a piece of cloth five cubits long, fold it into three pleats, and at the shoulder portion where the folds meet, leave a margin from the edge.
It should be about five finger-widths [in size]. One may place a square patch there, measuring five finger-widths on each side.
Prick around the four edges and pierce a small hole in the center to secure the garment’s loop. This loop may be made of cord or silk, with a thickness similar to that of a shirt’s loop.
It may be two finger-widths long. Tie it to form a firm knot; cut off the remainder. Pass the cord through the hole and pull it out toward the outside.
Cross the two ends in a "十" (ten) shape and tie them together to form two loops. Fasten a toggle inside this [loop].
As for the overlapping section at the chest, attach toggles along the edge, just like the toggers on a shirt; such is the method. Toggle-ties should also be applied to the lower hem of the garment.

One may wear it inverted at will; this is permitted by the Noble Ones. At both ends, the corners should be removed for a distance of about eight finger-widths, and a loop and a toggle should be provided on each side.
These are required for the time of eating: one should fold the robe back over the chest and fasten the toggles together; this constitutes the essential rule.
Whenever one is within the monastery, or when facing the assembly, one must never have the toggles fastened, nor employ the method of draping the robe over the shoulders.
If one travels abroad or enters the houses of laypeople, one must fasten the ties; at other times, it is sufficient merely to drape the robe over the shoulder.
When attending to private affairs, one may fold the robe back over the shoulder as one pleases. However, when in the presence of a venerable person, one must maintain proper decorum:

take the right corner of the robe and drape it broadly over the left shoulder, letting it hang behind the back rather than resting it upon the elbow. If one wishes to fasten the ties, one should do so.
One must then drape it over both shoulders, tuck the fastening inside the collar, and turn it behind the shoulder so that it does not slip off.
With a corner resting on the shoulder, the robe encircles the neck, with both sleeves hanging down from below; one corner hangs down in front—this is the image of King Aśoka.
This is precisely according to the proper form. When going out, one should hold an umbrella; one’s appearance and deportment should be pleasing.

This is the method for wearing the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) in accordance with the teachings and in a neat manner (the method for donning robes has long been lost; therefore, I have briefly set forth its general outline. Those who delight in the True Dharma should restore it to its original form). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:
"When wearing the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), one should not perform manual labor, walk on the road, sit with the robe wrapped around the thighs, or lie down while wearing it."
When prostrating while naked or wearing only a single garment, do not let the cloth brush against the ground.
Do not wrap it around the knees, nor sit or lie upon the two lower robes. If no other object is available, it is permitted to use them as a cushion for sitting or lying;
there is no offense. In putting on clothing, one should abandon three types of mentalities: first, the mind that delights in adornment; second, the mind that uses [the robe] with contempt.
Third is the mind that seeks fame through hypocrisy: wearing shabby clothes falsely in order to make others believe one possesses virtue and conduct.
These three types of mind should not be cultivated; rather, one should seek only dyed garments, obtaining whatever suffices for the body, in accordance with the Great Master’s teaching.
In cultivating wholesome qualities, one should give rise to five kinds of mentalities: first, knowing the proper measure; using things with due consideration so as not to cause damage or waste.
Second, knowing the proper intervals; one should not wear a single garment continuously, for it will become foul-smelling and quickly tear. Third, knowing how to reflect and examine.
First, know the source: it is extremely difficult to obtain. Second, cultivate a mind of gratitude. Third, when making use of them, do not engage in unrighteousness. Fourth, know the proper time:
use them in accordance with the seasons of cold and heat, and in moderation. Fifth, know the number: the thirteen requisites are sufficient to sustain the body.

To accumulate and store many robes is to increase greed and neglect one's practice. (The thirteen items are: the three robes, the sitting mat, the lower garment, the secondary lower garment, the armpit-covering cloth, the secondary armpit-covering cloth, the body-wiping cloth, the face-wiping cloth, the hair-cutting cloth, the wound-covering cloth, and the medicine-money robe.
If the seams or edges of a robe are torn or damaged, one should patch them with material or bind them with thread.
If one sees that there is a hole, it should be patched. If it is completely rotted and beyond repair, it should be made into a lamp wick;
or it may be chopped into pieces, mixed with cow dung to form mud, and used to fill the holes in pillars or to plaster walls.
When used in this manner, it causes the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) from which the donor has relinquished their gift to increase spontaneously.

Even for robes in such a state of decay, the Buddha did not permit them to be discarded lightly. Nowadays, there are those who hang the robes of deceased bhikṣus upon trees, claiming that spirits, birds, and magpies will thereby receive benefit. Even if they are robes of high value and fine quality, they are left to wither naturally under the wind and sun;

hung so densely that they fill the trees, they are most unseemly and strike the eyes of the laity with alarm. Such erroneous traditions have come to this extreme. However, regarding the clothing and belongings of the deceased, it is clearly stated in the Vinaya that the community should collectively perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to divide them. Why do you not examine this carefully?
To rely on one's own views is to practice with false delusions.
○ *Saṃkakṣikā* (or *saṃghāṭī*;
the latter is a corruption): this is a Sanskrit term. It is translated here as "covering the shoulders" (*fùzhǒn*) and also as "concealing the armpits" (*yǎnyè*).
Vertically, it measures two *hasta*; horizontally, five *hasta*. The Buddha established this rule fearing that the three robes (*tricīvara*) might become soiled.

As for the method of wearing it: one should expose the right shoulder and cross it over the left shoulder. It is to be worn constantly within the dwelling, together with the lower skirt (*nivasana*) alone.

When going outside to pay respects to the Honored One, one may add other garments as appropriate. This is the fundamental protocol of the śramaṇa. Since the Dharma flowed eastward to this land, the monks have all followed this practice. [Since] the Sage passed away...

At that time, [the robes] were distant [from the Indian style] and resembled secular clothing; they were worn with sleeves. As for the *pianshan* (partial shirt), it was also a garment manufactured in this region.
This was because when the Wei Emperor invited monks into the palace for offerings, the palace ladies saw that the monks bared their right shoulders and did not consider it proper.
They subsequently fashioned the *pianshan* and offered it to the monks, sewing it onto the left side of the *saṃkakṣikā* (undershirt). Consequently, it was named "partial" (*pien*).
Regarding the *shān* (shirt): today, while the name *zhīzhī* (undergarment) remains hidden, that which is called the "two-sleeved" garment is termed the *piānshān*.
If one wishes to make it, one must open the back seam and cut away the collar; only then does it preserve the original form of the Wei dynasty regulations.
The *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* (also called *nivāsana*; in the Tang language, "skirt") measures five cubits in width and two cubits in length.
When putting it on, once it has been wrapped around the body, lift it so that it passes above the navel; then, with the right hand, pull the upper corner of the left side inward.
Draw it toward the right side of the waist. For the left side, take the outer edge of the upper skirt and cover the left flank.
With both hands at both sides, lift them to make it even and level, keeping the center perfectly straight; this immediately forms three pleats.
Next, with both hands, gather each side toward the waist, folding all three layers together and tucking them behind. Lift each corner by three finger-widths and tuck them both in.
Direct it toward the spine and cause it to descend into the waist to a depth of about three finger-widths. Even if the sash has not yet been tied, it will remain on the body and not fall off.
Afterwards, using a sash or belt approximately five cubits (*hasta*) in length, hook it at the center, lift it toward below the navel, and smooth it over the upper edge of the skirt.
Draw it back toward the rear in two parallel rows, cross it over in front, and pull it out; then, pull it to the left and right respectively.
Using one hand, press down on both sides and wrap the two cords three times; if they are too long, cut them off, and if too short, add more.

The ends of the cords and bands must not be tied with decorative ribbons. This is called wearing the skirt in a perfectly neat manner, which constitutes the ritual protocol of the Sarvāstivāda school.
However, the four schools differ in their methods of wearing the skirt to distinguish themselves; this [method] belongs to the Mūlasarvāstivāda school.
In that case, both sides are folded outward. According to the Mahāsāṃghika school, the right skirt is gathered at the left side and tucked inward so as not to let it fall;
the way Western women wear their skirts is no different from this.
The Sarvāstivāda and Sammitīya schools follow the same regulation, differing only in that they turn the skirt outward straight and tuck it sideways.
For nuns, the rules follow those of the monks; there is no separate category at all. Thus, the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"Since they have no loops or straps, when they are about to put on the garment, they gather the cloth into pleats and fasten it with a cord. As for the pleats, each school differs;
as for the color, yellow and red vary. Its correct name is *nivāsana*; the old term 'nirvāṇa-saṅgha' is a corruption."

*Niśīdana*, *niśīdana*. This is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "sitting mat" (*zuòjù*). It is also called the "cloth for sitting according to [the occasion]" (*suízuò yī*) or the "cloth for following the feet" (*suízú yī*).

This means that because one must carry it along for convenience when sitting or lying down, it must not be separated from oneself. The Buddha said: "It is for the sake of the body and for the sake of the robes."
It was permitted for use as bedding; therefore, its possession was prescribed. Its length is two *vitasti* (hand-spans) of the Buddha, and its width is one and a half *vitasti*.
An additional half *vitasti* may be added to both the length and the width. One *vitasti* of the Buddha corresponds to one chi and eight cun.
Furthermore, it is said that one *vitasti* of the Buddha is equivalent to three *vitasti* of an ordinary person. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the length should be four chi and five cun.
The circumference is three chi and six cun. The length of the base section is five chi and four cun, and its width is two chi and seven cun.
As for its extension, it increases in length but not in width. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "To extend it by one span (*vitasti*)."
Cut it into three parts. Join the long ends together. As for the remaining one part, attach it to the four corners; if not, that is acceptable.
In the present day, people apply [the cloth] along the four edges and attach it to the four corners; this is based on that [original practice].

To call the four corners the "Four Heavenly Kings" is an extreme error. The Tripitaka Master Yijing stated: "The intention behind this regulation was originally to provide a protective lining for bedding. Fearing that there might be..."
It must not be damaged, nor should it be intended for any other use. Furthermore, its size should be equal to one's own body, with an additional span (vitasti) remaining at the top;

this is precisely what corresponds to a bedding mat (*śayanāsana*). If its dimensions are too small, it will be unfit to serve as a substitute for a bed, nor can it be spread on the ground for prostration, which would deeply violate the original ritual protocol.
If one intentionally contravenes the holy regulations, who shall take responsibility for the transgression? — *Neifa zhuan* (Biographies of the Inner Dharma).
It is said: After prostrating, one should spread out one’s sitting mat (*niṣīdana*). This practice is not seen among the people of the Five Indias.

As for what is required, it is intended solely for the time of sleeping and lying down, in order to protect the felt mats and seats of others. If using another’s property, whether new or old, one must invariably provide a protective layer.

If it is one’s own property, a layer is not required when it is already worn. One must ensure that no defilement occurs and that the faithful offerings (*śraddhā-deya*) are not damaged. The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:
A bhikṣu should not go outside without his sitting mat (niṣīdana). One who violates this incurs an offense of transgression (duṣkṛta).
If he intends to return immediately but encounters other circumstances such that he cannot return in time, he may stay overnight there;

however, he must not travel at night. He should borrow a substitute from a fellow practitioner of the holy life (sabrahmacārin) to serve the purpose; if none is available, he should take [a portion] of seven...
The *cīvara* (robe) is folded into four layers to serve as a substitute for mats and bedding; one sleeps little and remains awake until dawn.
As for the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), it should be made of two layers and dyed to a neutral color (*kāsāya*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A new one shall consist of two layers."
Therefore, the four heavy offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*) should not be committed alone. If one has previously received [the precepts], they should not be abandoned.
The *Kun-ga-lun* (Vinaya-sūtra) states: "If one stays overnight [without the seat], there is no need to abandon it; one need only perform the confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one wishes to make a new sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), one should take a piece from the old one measuring one span (*vitasti*) in length and breadth and patch it onto the new one in order to achieve the color of deterioration (*rañjana*). If there is no old one...
That is all. The *Śīla-hetupratyaya-sūtra* states: "Because of grasping, one relies on the four edges, thereby disturbing the color.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "The reason for patching is to ensure durability.

If there is no whole [piece], one should collect various materials extensively to patch it (since it is for the sake of durability, patching within [the existing material] is also permissible). The *Śīlamaṇḍala-sūtra* states: "The *niṣīdana* is like a stupa having..."
This is the foundation. Your receiving of the precepts now establishes the foundation for the fivefold Dharma-body. This is because the fivefold [Dharma-body] is accomplished through the precepts.
If you do not have a sitting mat upon which to sit your body, then the fivefold [qualities of] concentration and wisdom will have no basis from which to arise.
The remaining ritual procedures are as detailed in the Vinaya.
*Pātra-pātra* is the Sanskrit term;
it is translated here as *pātra*. Its meaning is "receptacle" (*yingqi*). This refers to the fact that its substance, color, and dimensions all accord with the Dharma.
As for the substance, it is made of clay or iron. As for the color, it is blackened or reddened by fumigating it with hemp seeds, apricot kernels, and the like.
Their colors may be like those of a peacock’s throat or a pigeon. They vary in size;

the large ones hold three *dǒu*, and the small ones hold one and a half *dǒu* (according to the Tang *dǒu*, a large bowl holds one *dǒu* and a small bowl holds five *shēng*; according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, a large bowl holds three *Qīn shēng* and a small bowl holds one and a half *shēng*).
One must not draw the svastika symbol on the bowl, nor write one's own name upon it. One is not permitted to keep bowls made of gold, silver, copper, or tin, as these are the vessels of laypeople.
One is not permitted to keep wooden bowls, as these are the vessels of non-Buddhists. However, one is permitted to make a bowl bag.
One should wear a shoulder-bag while going on alms-round. During ordinary times, one should construct a bowl-case to store the alms-bowl within.
If one is ill, the use of a spoon and chopsticks is permitted; in Sanskrit these are called *kuryara*, which here means "utensils accompanying the bowl.
These include spoons, chopsticks, and ladles (*kañci*). A *kañci* is a shallow iron bowl, now commonly referred to as a *dizi*.
This is an error. The Vinaya states: "A *kañcika* [ladle] may be placed in a small bowl; a small bowl in a medium bowl; and a medium bowl in a large bowl.
Such items as these are all permitted to be kept. Furthermore, it is permitted to keep vessels for drinking gruel and vessels for drinking water, such as bowls and cups;
however, after midday, they must necessarily be scrubbed clean with ash and washed until no oily odor of food remains before they are permitted for use.
Drinking Water (The Method for Incensing the Alms Bowl. Fully recorded in the Vinaya. *Jian* pronounced as *qián*; *zhi* pronounced as *zī*; *dì* pronounced as *xùn*).
○ *Bōlisuóluófǎnà* (濾囊), in Sanskrit: *parisrāvana*. This is translated as "water-strainer. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Upon receiving full ordination..."
Having completed the full precepts (*upasampadā*), one must necessarily possess a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*) and a ritual water-pitcher (*kuṇḍikā*).
When traveling, one should carry the water-strainer; if one lacks it, one must at least hold onto a corner of the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).

When examining water, one should not look with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), nor should one have someone with impaired vision examine it. When examining it, one must do so with a sincere mind; one must not...

It must be very quick; it should not take too long—only as long as it takes for a great elephant to turn around once. If there are no insects, one may use it; if there are insects, one should strain it before using it.
If the insects are extremely minute, one must not use the water to wash one's hands or face, nor for defecation or urination.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "Whenever one observes water, starting from sunrise until the appearance of the dawn light has not yet emerged—"

Come; all shall follow and partake. One should know that there are five kinds of water-strainers (*parisrāvaṇa*): first, the square strainer (*caturaśra-parisrāvaṇa*), which requires fine, dense silk (one or two chi in size, varying according to the occasion;
if the material is coarse or thin, it is fundamentally unfit for use); second, the *dharmagaḍuka* (the "Dharma-flask," also known as the "yin-yang flask"); third, the *kuṇḍikā*.

[This is called a water-strainer (*karakapaṭa*). It is made by stretching silk over the mouth [of a jar], tying a fine cord around its neck, and submerging it in water so that half the mouth protrudes. Once full, one draws it out; furthermore, one must inspect it for insects, and only when none are present may it be used. 4. The Water-Straining Cloth (*cullaka*): Made from silk, it is a small, circular strainer. 5.
The Corner-of-the-Robe Strainer (*kaṭhina-koṇa-cullaka*): Take a square piece of fine silk about one *tala* in size; it may be tied to the mouth of a jar or placed over the mouth of a bowl.

It is required when filtering water for alms, and is not the corner of a *kāṣāya*. These various types of strainers are all currently in use in the West. Out of compassion, the Great Master [Śāntarakṣita] provided them to aid sentient beings. If even eating meat is severed as a mark of great compassion, how could killing living beings ever lead to Buddhahood? Practitioners must therefore specifically maintain and protect these rules.
This is for the benefit of oneself and others). Tripitaka Master Yi Jing stated: "The water filter is counted among the six requisites;
it must not be left behind. If one travels three or five *li*, one cannot go without the filter. If one knows that a monastery does not strain its water, it is improper to consume food there."
Dying of thirst on a long journey serves as a sufficient mirror for reflection. The holy teaching of the Tathāgata takes compassion as its foundation.

Among the precepts he established, there are those that are natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and those that are prohibitive transgressions (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*). Prohibitive transgressions are light according to the specific circumstances; natural transgressions, however, ought by principle to be treated as grave.

Within the category of natural transgressions, taking life is the foremost. Therefore, the wise should especially protect [life]. If one regards this as a minor matter, [one will suffer the aforementioned consequences].

Furthermore, what more could constitute a grave offense? Suppose one has mastered the Tripitaka, attained the realization of the four dhyānas through meditation, constantly contemplates non-arising, and clarifies the mind in the principle of emptiness;
yet, if one does not protect life and fails to practice according to the teachings, in the end one cannot escape the Buddha’s reproach.
Regarding the first of the ten evil deeds, who can take its retribution upon themselves? Moreover, there are those who cause others to plow fields and plant crops.
Seeking meager profit, one fails to see the great transgression. Both land and water creatures are harmed, and countless beings are killed.
As for such guilt and fault, what can be done? It is as if one were bound hand and foot at the gate of the underworld, left to the disposal of others.
Thus, a sutra says: "A person who kills shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; even if they manage to become human again, they will have a short life and many ailments."
How lamentable is this suffering! Who shall endure it? If there be one capable of acting on its behalf, how excellent, how most excellent!

This may truly be called the final dharma age of Śākyamuni; together we shall bind the causes for compassionate mindfulness, and when Maitreya first attains enlightenment, we shall all realize the fruit of non-arising.
(The three robes, the alms bowl, and the water filter—these are the six essential requisites for a bhikṣu.)

*Muñci* (or *muñci*), sometimes transcribed as *junzhijia* (君持迦), is a term of Indic origin meaning "flask" (*kamaṇḍalu*). The *Xiyuji* (Record of the Western Regions) states that this refers to the bathing flask (*snāna-kamaṇḍalu*).
According to the *Vinaya-ksudraka-vastu*, nuns possess the *muñci*, while monks possess the "bathing jar," which refers to a double-mouthed bathing jar. (*Vinaya-ksudraka-vastu*)
It is said: "The *kuṇḍikā* (water flask) is placed in a bundle; the mouth of the *śīrṣaka* (washing pitcher) is open. The *Nanhai Jiguai Neifa Zhuan* states: "There are two types of flasks.

Those for purification are all made of earthenware or porcelain; they are intended for use at improper times [for drinking], and one must hold them only with clean hands. They must be kept in a pure location."
Regarding the *spraṣṭavya* (the vessel for contact): it may be made of either copper or iron, as required for the needs of excretion and urination.
It should be held wherever it touches the hand, and may be placed wherever it is touched. As for the method of making this jar: the opening must be wide and the mouth narrow;

a pointed spout should protrude from the top, about two finger-widths high, with a small hole at the top as thick as a copper chopstick, through which one may drink water. On the side, a separate circular opening should be cut.
The opening: seal the mouth of the vessel and erect a spout two finger-widths high; the opening should be about the size of a coin. Water should be added through this point.
It can hold two or three *sheng*; a small one is of no use.
○ *Śikya* is a term from the Sanskrit language; in this [language], it is called *khakkhara*, which means "staff of sound.

Because it produces a *khak-khak* sound when shaken, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* calls it the "Sound Staff" (*śabdadaṇḍa*), establishing its name based on its sound. As for its substance, it may be made of copper or iron and is not restricted to tin (*śikya*). — Yijing.
The Tripitaka Master says: As for what is called a *khakkhara* (錫杖), the Sanskrit term is *khikkhira*, which carries the meaning of "emitting sound.

When ancient translators rendered it as "錫杖" (*xizhang*), they intended to capture the sense of a staff that produces a metallic ringing sound; thus, the terms "錫" (*xi*) and "杖" (*zhang*) were used according to their respective connotations.
Upon direct observation in the Western Regions, the *khakkhara* carried there consists of a single iron ring at its head, capable of holding two or three [beads].

Nutriment by mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*): This refers to that which, through the power of intention, sustains and nourishes the sense faculties and the life-force, as in the case of fish, turtles, snakes, frogs, and the like.

Nutriment by consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*): As in the hells, among animals, and for the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), all use consciousness as their sustaining nutriment.

The Vinaya has four meanings: first, it is the level ground within the Buddha-dharma, from which all myriad virtues arise;

By practicing humility, one attains four virtues: first, one distances oneself from the miserable realms and does not undergo rebirth as an animal; second, one is not subjected to contempt or disparagement;

first, calculate the amount of labor expended and measure the distance from which it was brought—for instance, even a single bowl of rice.

First, when working as a laborer, one’s sweat flows profusely. Second, one should reflect upon whether one’s own virtuous conduct is complete or deficient regarding the worthiness of receiving offerings;

that is, one remains free from greed, hatred, and delusion. Fourth, [food] is truly a wholesome medicine for treating the withered body, meaning that because of the ailments of hunger and thirst, food must be taken as medicine.
Fifth, one accepts this food for the sake of accomplishing the Way; that is to say, if one does not eat, one will fall ill, and the work of the Way will not be accomplished.
There are five blessings in not eating after midday: first, little sexual desire; second, little sleep; third, attaining single-mindedness; fourth, little flatulence;

In begging for alms, one should avoid five types of households: first, those that make proclamations; second, the households of *caṇḍālas*;

In Sanskrit, it is *dantadhāvana*, which means "tooth-wood. One must not use wood from varnish trees, poisonous trees, or Bodhi trees. Its branches should be used.
Paper mulberry (*Broussonetia*), peach, locust, willow, and the root of *Cirsium* (蒼耳)—those that are bitter, astringent, and pungent are preferred.
They should be one *vitasti* (a span) long at most, or four fingers long at shortest; some say they should be twelve inches long at most, or six inches at shortest.
The large ones are like the little finger, and the small ones are like chopsticks. Chew about half an inch of the tip until it becomes like cotton, then slowly brush the teeth and gums.
Rinse the mouth thoroughly with water two or three times and discard it without swallowing. One must not chew the bark alone, nor that from which the bark has been removed.
One must not chew mixed leaves, nor two or three strips at once. There are five faults in not chewing *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks):

There are five benefits to chewing [tooth-sticks]. These are the reverse of the aforementioned [disadvantages]. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states:

"Every morning at dawn, one must chew a tooth-stick to clean the teeth and scrape the tongue, ensuring it is done according to the Dharma. Only after rinsing and becoming pure may one perform acts of reverence.
If one does otherwise, both receiving and offering salutations will result in fault. Furthermore, when chewing, if one draws near to a person of superior status..."
One should cover the mouth with the left hand while using the tooth-stick. Once finished, one should break it apart, bend it, and scrape the tongue.

Having done so, both [the stick and the debris] may be washed and discarded in a secluded place. Whenever discarding the tooth-stick, if water is spat from the mouth, or if mucus or saliva is discharged, one must snap the fingers three times;
or at other times, one should clear the throat twice. If one does not do so, one incurs an offense by discarding it.
If food remains between the teeth or a film of grease persists upon the tongue, one must discard the saliva externally before rinsing again with pure water.
If the designated time for this has passed, one further commits the offense of eating at an improper time (*vikālabhojana*).

However, according to the custom of the Western lands (India), chewing tooth-sticks is a constant practice; even three-year-old children are taught to do so. Thus, both the sacred teachings and worldly customs are in accord.
Regarding the benefits: the Vinaya states that if one is traveling and tooth-sticks cannot be readily obtained, one should use soap powder (*śīrṣaka*), earth, or other such substances.
